Tennessee officials attempted to execute Pike on Sept. 30 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, but she survived two doses of pentobarbital during the lethal injection procedure.
Despite severe arm injuries from the procedure, Pike remains handcuffed and shackled to her hospital bed, with swollen, burned, and blistered arms requiring ongoing medical treatment.
Lee ordered a third-party review of the failed execution, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned following the incident; a court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 7.
Pike faces a long recovery process, as her survival of lethal injection chemicals remains unprecedented in execution history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

summary: On Tuesday, Oct 6, 2026, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to Belgian-American particle physicist Francis Halzen for "decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

Halzen's research at the IceCube, which the committee described as "ghostly messages from space," has fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe and the nature of high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, which is shared among winners if there are several; the award was established under the will of Alfred Nobel to honor scientific achievement.

Nobel medals will be presented by Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, followed by an elaborate banquet at Stockholm City Hall.

This announcement follows Monday's medicine prize, with the chemistry award scheduled for Wednesday as part of the annual Nobel Prizes recognition cycle honoring global scientific and literary achievements.
title: Nobel Prize in Physics Awarded to Francis Halzen for Astronomy Breakthroughs

summary: Dr. Karl Deisseroth, a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator, won the Nobel Prize for medicine early Monday for his work developing optogenetics, a field combining light and genes to control neurons in living brains.

Deisseroth shared the prize with researchers Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel in Germany for their collaborative development of optogenetics, a breakthrough that switches neurons on and off using light and genetic techniques.

After receiving the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm, Deisseroth celebrated at his Stanford home while his wife, Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, joined him as Stanford University staff coordinated remote interviews throughout the night.
When media attention intensified, Deisseroth paused the interviews to request a break starting at 6:30 a.m. because his children needed school lunches before leaving for the day.

Deisseroth emphasized his dual identity, saying "For me, I'm a physician-scientist. I care about patients and my patients who have autism, who have depression." He added he cares about understanding how the brain works.
title: Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to three scientists for their work ‘concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’

Twelve B-1B Lancer bombers had been stationed at Fairford since March, serving as a key launch point for strikes against Iran. The withdrawal follows an investigation into an alleged plot targeting the base.

Police arrested five British nationals and one dual Iranian citizen regarding the alleged scheme. US officials claimed an individual linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps recruited the suspects, though British authorities have not confirmed this finding.

The Defense Department stressed it remains on alert to employ "global strike capability" from US territory, noting the return does not eliminate long-range strike options. It remains unclear whether replacement aircraft will be sent to Fairford.

Following the base's use in Iran operations, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officials previously warned that facilities supporting US strikes could be considered legitimate targets. British investigations into the alleged plot and potential foreign state involvement are continuing.
title: US Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack

summary: On Wednesday, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

The laureates solved a century-old chemical mystery by determining how homochirality emerges spontaneously. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.

Kagan is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in France, while Soai, 95, is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science. The pair will share a 12 million Swedish kronor award comprising a diploma, medal, and cash prize.

This announcement marks the third of six Nobel awards this year, following recognition for physiology or medicine and physics earlier this week. Literature, peace, and economic sciences awards continue through Monday.

These discoveries enable chemists to drive reactions leading to homochirality, providing a foundation to address global challenges like climate change. The Academy's recognition reflects the fundamental significance of asymmetric synthesis in modern chemistry.
title: Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai

summary: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens an "Unacceptable Risk" on Wednesday, urging OpenAI to cease marketing the tool to minors until it provides a safer experience.

Researchers tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds to evaluate safety features OpenAI launched in August, finding the tool fails to function as marketed despite company commitments to prioritize teen safety.

Testers found parental alerts failed to trigger during hour-long conversations about self-harm, while students could easily bypass "Study Mode" using a "Show me the answer" button, contradicting the company's "stronger built-in safety protections."

OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield argued the report's methodology was flawed, claiming testing occurred before parental accounts fully linked, though the company maintains it is "deeply committed to teen safety."

The report recommends OpenAI prohibit adolescents from using the platform until it can "offer a safe, developmentally appropriate experience," noting the tool failed requirements of California's Adam's Law, effective July 2027.
title: ChatGPT's 'Teen Mode' Is Unsafe for Students, Report Concludes

summary: On Tuesday, OpenAI released 722 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts in a public GitHub repository, organized into 372 research families spanning number theory and theoretical computer science.

The release adds to a growing body of AI-generated results the mathematical community is still processing, though mathematician Terence Tao has previously criticized the "insane" pace of such breakthroughs.
title: OpenAI's largest math release tackles 4,000 problems with Lean proofs

summary: Jamaal Howard is set to be executed on Wednesday in Texas by lethal injection for the 2000 fatal shooting of convenience store clerk Vickie Swartout, marking the nation's 30th execution this year.
In the 2000 robbery, Howard fatally shot Swartout at a store in Silsbee, Texas; court records show the then-20-year-old Howard took $114 and a carton of cigarettes before fleeing.
Surveillance video presented at trial captured Howard shooting Swartout, with the crime occurring in Silsbee, 161 kilometers northeast of Houston; Howard was convicted of capital murder.
Howard's attorneys have filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, arguing he is intellectually disabled; the state maintains he has not presented sufficient evidence to meet disability requirements.

Texas has executed six people this year with two more scheduled after Howard, while Florida has carried out 16 executions, the most of any state following Tennessee's failed execution attempt involving Christa Pike.
title: Texas set to execute man for fatally shooting a convenience store clerk during robbery in 2000

summary: Satellite imagery from The Planet Labs reveals widespread demolition across Gaza, with Israeli forces systematically razing towns and districts using bulldozers and explosives since the ceasefire deal reached a year ago.

Israel maintains control over around 60% of the territory, saying it demolishes buildings to prevent Hamas militants from using them, while Gaza's population remains squeezed into about 40% of the tiny territory.

In the north, Jabaliya's refugee camp and the Awda Hospital Complex were reduced to rubble, while Beit Hanoun and Shijaiya now consist of leveled apartment towers; at least 50 military outposts stand throughout Israeli-held areas.

With 2 million Palestinians displaced, survivors endure profound losses; Shadi Barawi, a 35-year-old amputee barber, balances on crutches to earn money while Najwa Abu Eita lives in a tent after losing her daughter.

A U.N.-appointed expert warned in a February report that the scale of destruction could constitute a crime against humanity, yet large-scale reconstruction remains stalled as Israel and Hamas have failed to reach a disarmament agreement.
title: Satellite Images Show Widespread Gaza Demolitions by Israeli Forces

summary: On Monday, Lewis and Clark County District Court Judge Mike Menahan ruled that Montana's requirement for voters to write their birth year on absentee ballot envelopes is unconstitutional, finding it disenfranchised nearly 6,000 voters since 2025.

The 2025 Legislature created the requirement, proposed by Rep. Braxton Mitchell, to prevent voter fraud; Disability Rights Montana and Big Sky 55+ challenged the legislation, arguing it discarded lawful votes without evidence of fraud.

In Billings, Judge Menahan noted the 2025 mayoral race was decided by 200 votes, while 627 ballots were excluded because they lacked birth years, demonstrating the requirement's potential to alter election outcomes.

Consequently, 2026 general election ballot envelopes missing a birth year will not be rejected; Montana Secretary of State Christie Jacobsen defended the law, while spokesperson Richie Melby called the ruling "mass confusion" during voting .

In a press release, Big Sky 55+ praised the decision, with chairperson Terry Minow stating it ensures democracy remains healthy by counting all votes; the state has not yet indicated if it will appeal.
title: State judge strikes down Montana’s ballot envelope birth year requirement

Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said, while the AI-related building boom is inflationary.

Finance ministers of 191 IMF-World Bank member countries will gather in Bangkok next week to assess global stability, as Georgieva noted AI-related benefits are "highly uneven across the world" and threaten to widen economic inequality.

Urging policymakers to avoid delaying action, Georgieva stated, "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," as fiscal space is "crying out for replenishment."

Citing Amara's Law, Georgieva said the world is traversing a critical transition between today's AI-related building boom and tomorrow's AI-related benefits, representing the period of maximum risk as triple forces challenge growth this decade.
title: IMF chief warns energy shock, growing debt and AI risks threaten global growth

summary: President Donald Trump approved the firing squad execution of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan on Monday, October 5, 2026, following a recommendation from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced.
Hasan killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at the Fort Hood Soldier Readiness Processing Center in 2009, later describing his actions as retaliation for U.S. wars in the Muslim world.

Acting Secretary of the U.S. Army Adam Telle announced Tuesday that the execution is set for December 3, marking the first U.S. military execution since 1961, when the military last hanged Army Pvt. John Bennett.

Although Trump's approval initiates procedural steps, Hasan could still file a habeas corpus appeal in civilian federal courts, which historically have delayed military executions for years and could stall the process beyond December 3.

Whether the first military execution in 65 years occurs in 2027 or later depends on a federal district judge in Kansas, while Parnell noted the Army will set the location, stating, 'Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.
title: Firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan scheduled for December

California Governor Gavin Newsom called the President "deranged," while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass labeled the comments "dangerous," arguing they treated residents as expendable collateral damage.
Tensions between the administration and California intensified as Newsom linked the rhetoric to Trump's deployment of 700 Marines to the state last year during immigration enforcement clashes.
The White House dismissed the backlash as a "media freakout" that "is not rooted in reality," while Representative Kevin Kiley joined Democrats in questioning the President's comments.
With control of Congress on the line in November, the midterms will weigh heavily on the final two years of the President's term as voters decide if the election matters.
title: Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the early review of eight ABC licenses as a “retaliatory effort” and “crackdown,” emphasizing alleged censorship, Trump’s criticism of Jimmy Kimmel and The View, and a “chilling effect” on editorial decisions; vivid phrases like “head on a guillotine” heighten alarm.
Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds regulatory authority and “jurisdiction,” portraying censorship claims as Disney’s allegation while emphasizing limits on court intervention.
Center coverage presents a restrained legal test, noting judicial “skepticism” but also additional briefing and no immediate ruling.
The dividing line is whether the review signals political punishment or ordinary oversight, reflecting wider disputes over executive power, media legitimacy, and free speech.
summary: On Tuesday, Disney and ABC sought to block the Federal Communications Commission's order requiring early renewal proceedings for eight broadcast stations, with the network's attorney arguing the move creates an ongoing "chilling effect."
FCC Chair Brendan Carr ordered the review after President Donald Trump repeatedly called to revoke ABC's licenses, citing content grievances regarding comedian Jimmy Kimmel and The View.

ABC lead attorney Beth Wilkinson described the threat of losing licenses as a "death penalty" for stations, noting the network has already altered content, such as cutting political clips from The View to avoid FCC scrutiny.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan heard arguments Tuesday but made no ruling, while FCC lawyers defended the move as a standard regulatory inquiry, arguing the network must exhaust administrative remedies before pursuing litigation.
Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, warned the FCC's actions represent a significant threat to journalism, calling them an effort to "intimidate the press.
title: ABC to Federal Judge: Trump’s FCC Is Holding Our Head on a ‘Guillotine’

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the HHS legal team as a threat to vulnerable “migrant kids,” warning it could “deprive” them of independent counsel and heighten “risk of deportation,” while placing the move against the 2008 representation system.

Right-Leaning coverage emphasizes intended legal “advice and counsel,” a written “independence firewall,” and critics’ concerns as potential—not proven—harm, though phrases like “sound the alarm” add alarmist emotion.
Center coverage mainly presents the controversy and independence question without either side’s fuller context.

The dividing line is whether government lawyers signify protection or conflicted enforcement; all agree the team represents unaccompanied children and has sparked concern, reflecting broader immigration and institutional-trust divides.
summary: Last week, The Trump administration announced creation of an in-house legal team within the Health and Human Services Department to provide direct legal advice and counsel to unaccompanied migrant children through the new Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division.

This decision follows the administration cutting ties with the Acacia Center, which managed 24,000 cases through a vast network of legal service providers. The government recently awarded a contract to Our Rescue worth up to $244 million.

Shaina Aber, executive director of the Acacia Center, argued the move creates conflicts of interest, stating it 'will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children's rights and well-being.' Critics contend placing legal representation inside the agency holding children violates independence standards.

Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, warned government-employed attorneys might encourage minors to accept voluntary departure. Young noted the child's lawyer, judge, and prosecutors seeking deportation would all be federal employees.

Sui Chung, executive director of Americans for Immigrant Justice, stated denying independent counsel is a 'fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises.' The division will operate under HHS general counsel direction, raising questions about zealous representation.
title: Trump administration to assign government lawyers to migrant kids’ cases, worrying advocates

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames childhood obesity as an urgent global-health crisis, stressing that cases “quadrupled,” affect roughly 170 million young people, and require “strict criteria” and a “high degree of caution” before GLP-1 use.

Right-Leaning coverage instead spotlights institutional limits—“no” drugs or surgery under 10, medication only after lifestyle programs have “failed”—and uses the colloquial “slimming pen,” while emphasizing mental-health support and personal behavior.
Center coverage presents a policy comparison, contrasting lifestyle measures with “popular weight-loss drugs” and distinguishing children from adults.
All agree on WHO guidance, lifestyle-first care, and restricted adolescent medication, reflecting wider tensions over medicalization, institutional authority, and individual responsibility.
summary: On Wednesday, The World Health Organization released its first global guidelines recommending diet, exercise, and counseling over weight-loss drugs for managing rising obesity among children and adolescents.
Obesity prevalence among those aged 5 to 19 has quadrupled since 1990; about 400 million people were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity.
For children under 10, WHO endorsed diet, physical activity, and behavioral support instead of medication, while adolescents aged 10 to 19 may consider drugs only after supervised interventions fail.
Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Saxenda are already approved for adolescents 12 and older in the United States and European Union, while bariatric surgery is an option after six months of failed treatment.

Luz Regil, director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, noted there is "currently insufficient evidence" on GLP-1 drugs, though researchers are monitoring efficacy trials for potential reassessment.
title: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight

bias: Left-Leaning coverage contextualizes Vance as a “longtime skeptic” of foreign wars taking a “leading role” in negotiations, while right-leaning framing stresses confrontation: “demands,” Iran’s 60% enrichment, and the rhetorical question “Why do you need…?” that casts Tehran’s position as suspect.
The left de-emphasizes the enrichment figure and Washington’s rejection of Iran’s offer; the right de-emphasizes Vance’s anti-intervention background.
Center coverage stays concise, attributing the “must” condition to Vance.
All emphasize a meaningful enrichment cut to end the seven-month war , revealing a shared focus on security and diplomacy amid broader divides over intervention and Iran’s intentions.
summary: On Monday, Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the seven-month war.

Complicating negotiations, Vance noted that Washington remains uncertain who holds decision-making authority in Tehran following the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, even while maintaining talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi.
The war's $3 billion monthly price tag and higher energy costs have created political liabilities for President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of next month's midterm elections.

Trump rejected Tehran's latest proposal and warned of intensifying military operations after the midterms, while Vance campaigned in Fairbanks for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.

Maintaining a firm stance, Vance stated the US will not "trade words for actions" regarding nuclear concessions, emphasizing that Iran must halt production of highly enriched fuel to demonstrate commitment to non-proliferation.
title: In interview, US Vice President Vance says Iran must cut nuclear enrichment to end war

bias: No left-leaning coverage is supplied; the contrast is chiefly between cautious center framing and skeptical right-leaning framing.

Center reports describe SpaceX “seeking” $40 billion—roughly $10 billion in loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt—to buy Nvidia chips, while stressing the report was not independently verified and portraying “insatiable demand” for AI computing.
Right coverage emphasizes an “AI boom” and competitive “race,” frames the deal as debt-heavy expansion, and uses loaded terms such as “record,” “taps,” and “SPV debt,” suggesting scale and risk.
Both highlight the $40 billion figure, Apollo’s involvement, Nvidia hardware, and AI infrastructure, reflecting shared focus amid differing attitudes toward financial exposure.
summary: SpaceX is seeking $40 billion in financing led by Apollo Global Management to purchase Nvidia chips, according to reports on Tuesday, underscoring demand for AI computing power.

The financing structure comprises about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, with Apollo expected to lead the deal and sell debt to investors including Pacific Investment Management.

Tech companies are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips, as worldwide expansion sends costs for land and power-generation equipment soaring.
Musk said in September his Memphis-area Colossus 2 cluster, holding 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, may more than double its count by year-end, with 220,000 GB300s due next week.

Following an August partnership where Nvidia tapped investment giants to source $500 billion for AI infrastructure, the SpaceX deal is expected to close in 2027, aligning with efforts to create dedicated capital pools for Nvidia customers.
title: SpaceX Seeks $40 Billion Apollo-Led Financing to Buy Nvidia Chips

bias: Coverage splits over whether Trump’s proposed federal gas-tax suspension is primarily economic relief or electoral damage control: left-leaning accounts emphasize high prices as a “risk” to Republicans before the midterms, while right-leaning narratives highlight “pain at the pump,” “bring prices down,” state tax cuts, and the 18.4-cent-per-gallon rate.

The right also spotlights the irony that Trump’s “own party shelved” a related bill, portraying intraparty tension; center coverage instead cautions that savings may be “modest” because drivers might not receive the full reduction.
All portray the policy as tentative, acknowledge elevated fuel costs, and connect the debate to consumer pressure and electoral politics .
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump said he is considering suspending the 18.4-cent federal gas tax, though he provided no specific details on the proposal.
Fuel prices have surged due to the US-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with conflicts impacting refineries in the Middle East and Russia.
Trump's approval rating sits at a record low 32%, and high costs pose a risk to the Republican Party in midterm elections where control of Congress is at stake.
Trump signed an executive order to expand access to tax-exempt diesel following a rally in Nebraska, aiming to address fuel costs for voters.
Waiving the federal gas tax requires legislation from Congress, an option Trump has previously expressed support for in recent months.
title: Trump Says His Administration Is Thinking About Suspending Federal Gas Tax

summary: Wednesday, October 7, 2026, marks the third anniversary of the war in the Gaza Strip, as Canadians with ties to the region navigate three years of grief, humanitarian crises, and uncertainty regarding loved ones trapped abroad.

Hamas launched a deadly attack on Israel three years ago, triggering a war that has killed more than 75,000 people in the Gaza Strip while creating widespread humanitarian suffering and regional instability.

Canadian Jacob Flickinger, a 33-year-old infantry veteran, was killed in an Israeli airstrike while working for World Central Kitchen; his mother, Sylvie Labrecque, said he "enjoyed very much to go work for these types of missions."

Edmonton resident Abusalim remains separated from her husband in Gaza, saying "My husband was starving, literally starving." The Immigration Department has stalled his visa by requiring biometric screening impossible to complete there.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand pledged to press for accountability after Israel's military prosecutor declined a criminal investigation, though critics fear Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has little incentive to address these concerns.
title: Anniversary of Gaza war marks 3 years of pain for Canadians with ties to Middle East

bias: The left-leaning account frames the episode as a correction, using “No” and “Palestinian suffering” to stress that Louis Menand mocked or questioned the book’s argument and that critics “misrepresented” his review.

Right-Leaning accounts instead foreground “brutal colonial system,” “colonialism,” and “platforming,” portraying publication of claims involving antisemitism and Jewish migration to Israel as prompting “backlash.” Thus, one side emphasizes skepticism and alleged distortion; the other emphasizes editorial legitimization of provocative claims.

Both agree on the book, the review, its discussion of Hebrew punctuation, colonialism, and migration, and ensuing online criticism, while revealing competing sensitivities over Palestinian suffering and historical interpretation.
summary: The New Yorker published Louis Menand’s review of Florence Hazrat’s book “On the Mark,” which examines punctuation’s role in Hebrew, language, and history.
Hazrat argues that Hebrew punctuation was connected to colonialism and helped create unity among Jews moving to Israel .
Menand described the book as “irreverent and delightfully intellectual” but criticized its central claim as an overreach.
Commentators including Daniel Sugarman, Isaac de Castro, and Dave Aronberg criticized the arguments and The New Yorker’s decision to publish the review.
title: New Yorker Review Criticized Over Claims Linking Hebrew Punctuation to Jewish Unity

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the ICC “arrest warrant,” “fugitive” language, and possible breaches of international law, portraying the overflight as evidence of impunity; right-leaning coverage instead stresses alleged “double standards,” Macron’s “fine speech,” and Canada’s “threatened arrest,” framing the episode as Western hypocrisy and unmet enforcement promises.
Center coverage uses “posed no obstacle” and explains the legal distinction between airspace transit, territorial entry, and ICC obligations, while noting that authorization was not endorsement.
The pivotal divide is whether the flight represents evasion of justice or lawful transit.
All perspectives emphasize Netanyahu’s warrant, the France /Canada crossings, and the gap between legal commitments and practical enforcement.
summary: On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew over Greece, Italy, France and Canada en route to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for his arrest.

The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza; Canada, Italy, France and Greece are ICC members legally obliged to enforce such warrants.

On Tuesday, the UK sent a spy plane to Israel, contradicting Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's earlier claim this month that the UK would "reset" its policy, just weeks after Miliband announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

French Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux defended the clearance as "in full conformity with international law," arguing the Rome Statute does not impose overflight obligations; UN special rapporteur Ben Saul disputed this, citing the Tokyo Convention 1963.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog warned UK sanctions would "be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation" as elections approach next month, while Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar warned, "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain.
title: France says ICC warrant posed no obstacle to Netanyahu overflight

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 2.5-meter gold statue as pointed satire and a political rebuke, using terms like “humiliated,” “Orange Plague,” and “King of Injustice” to emphasize ridicule, climate policy, and Trump’s broader conduct.
Right-Leaning coverage instead calls it “bizarre,” “mock,” and a “provocation,” spotlighting the left-wing parliamentary sponsor, institutional propriety, and possible EU-US tensions.
Center coverage de-emphasizes partisan conflict, mainly describing the artwork, location, and satirical climate critique.

The sharpest divide concerns whether Parliament hosted legitimate political art or partisan misuse of institutional space; still, all perspectives highlight the naked, gilded depiction, its provocative symbolism, and the artist’s criticism of Trump.
summary: A 2.5-meter satirical statue of USPresident Donald Trump was installed at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Titled "Orange Plague," the figure is coated in 23-karat gold and depicts the leader sitting on a man's shoulders.
Danishartist Jens Galschiot created the sculpture, also known as the "King of Injustice." Accompanying cards explain the figure is "sitting on the back of a man" who is sinking under the burden.

Left-Wing Danish European Parliament member Per Clausen invited the artist to display the work. Dismissing potential criticism, Clausen stated, "If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage."
Previously exhibited in other European cities and at the COP30 UN climate conference in Belem, Brazil, the statue remains at the parliament. Trump has offered no comment on the installation.

The artwork will remain at the parliament until Thursday. Cards near the piece reflect the artist's view on climate change, stating, "I would do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.
title: Gold Donald Trump statue appears at European Parliament

summary: On Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz commemorated the Oct. 7, 2023, anniversary in New York, celebrating the return of every hostage taken during the Hamas attack and insisting the violence must "never, ever happen again."

This year's commemoration marked a sharp shift from 2025, when 48 hostages, including two Americans, remained in Hamas tunnels; the living have returned to their families, and those murdered were brought home for proper burial.

Former hostage Eliya Cohen and Nova festival survivor Ziv Abud attended the event alongside television host Phil McGraw, who emphasized the lasting trauma and antisemitism facing Jewish communities since Oct. 7, 2023, was the deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

Waltz argued that the Oct. 7 attack backfired on Iran, noting the Abraham Accords are expanding while Israel and Arab nations now cooperate on defense, including Iron Dome technology protecting cities in the United Arab Emirates.

President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan and U.N. Security Council Resolution 2803, which passed 13-0, provide a framework for a Gaza without Hamas rule, demilitarization, and an international stabilization force, the ambassador said.
title: At UN's October 7th Commemoration, U.S.'s Waltz Says Attack on Israel 'Backfired on Iran'

summary: The NDP election campaign in British Columbia has shifted focus from Trump's threats to prioritize affordability, with NDP Leader David Eby emphasizing that voters on Oct. 24 must decide which party best supports families.
When NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22, he sought a "firebreak" against Trump's economic attacks and Trump-style politics threatening the province.

On Tuesday, Eby acknowledged not everyone shares his anxiety about Trump, stating, "Whether you believe and accept that Trump is making it much worse, it doesn't matter because you're still understanding that the cost of living is significant."
Despite differing views on the U.S. president, Eby maintained that Trump's actions continue to impact British Columbians, who prioritize affordable health care and cost of living.
With the provincial election on Oct. 24 approaching, Eby stressed that voters must determine which party can best support families during these challenging times.
title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby says not everybody shares his concerns about Trump
